descs.en: A merchant's daughter who keeps the books in secret. An auditor sent to find the errors. A dynasty-era love story built on trust and ledgers.

chapters.desc: She was taught to be invisible. She refused.
chapters.title: The Merchant's Daughter
chapters.content:
In the fourth year of the Minghua reign, when the silk trade ran from the eastern ports to the desert crossings and back again in a river of coin and cloth and carefully managed debt, Zhou Yinghua did her father's accounts in secret and better than he did them himself.

She was twenty-two. She had been taught to pour tea, to embroider, to walk with the careful grace expected of a merchant's daughter of good family. She had learned all of these things and performed them when required and found them, in honest moments, insufficient.

The accounts were different. The accounts were a language she had taught herself from her father's discarded ledgers, and in them she had found something that felt less like a skill and more like a language she had always known.

✦   ✦   ✦

She was fixing an especially bad miscalculation when the door opened and a voice said: "Those numbers are wrong."

She looked up. A man she did not know stood in the doorway — dusty from travel, plainly dressed, and very still, the way people become after years in places where moving was dangerous.

"I know," she said. "I'm correcting them."

He looked at the ledger. He looked at her. Something in his face changed. Not surprise, exactly. More like he had just realized this job would be more interesting than he'd thought.

"Your father sent me to review the accounts," he said.

"Then we'll be working together," said Zhou Yinghua, and turned back to the columns, and did not let him see that her hands were shaking, not from fear but from something stranger: the feeling of being caught doing something true.
chapters.epigraph: "A woman who knows the price of silk knows the price of everything — including herself."

chapters.desc: The mathematics of trade, trust, and risk.
chapters.title: Silk Road Arithmetic
chapters.content:
His name was Wei Congming and he had been, variously, a soldier, an inspector, a translator, and a man who could calculate the true value of a shipment by smell alone. He did not say these things. Zhou Yinghua found them out the way she found out most things: by watching, and keeping her conclusions to herself until she was sure.

They worked together for three weeks before either of them said anything that wasn't strictly about the accounts. In those three weeks, she corrected four of his calculations (tactfully) and he acknowledged three of the corrections (tersely) and they developed between them, without discussion, a system for dividing the work that was more efficient than anything her father had previously managed.

✦   ✦   ✦

"Why do you do it in secret?" he asked on the seventeenth evening, without looking up from his column.

She did not pretend to misunderstand. "Because if my father knew I was better at this than he is, he would stop letting me do it."

Wei Congming set down his brush. He looked at her for a long moment, and she could not tell what he was thinking.

"That," he said, "is the most pragmatic thing I've heard in three months."

She looked at him. "Is that a compliment?"

"In my experience," he said, picking up his brush again, "pragmatism is the highest compliment there is."
chapters.epigraph: "Every calculation is also a wager. The wise merchant knows which is which."
